title: Strategy and competition
summary: Where to play and how to win: markets, rivals, and the big bets that shape a product.

lessons.title: Where to play
teach: Strategy starts with two questions: where will we play (which users, which markets) and how will we win there?
Market size matters, but so does fit. A huge market where you have no edge is a bad choice.
Many winners start with a small group they can serve better than anyone, then expand.

questions.prompt: Why did Meesho focus on small town shoppers first?
options: Amazon and Flipkart served them less well, and price mattered most to them
questions.explain: An underserved group with clear needs (low prices, social selling) gave Meesho an edge.

questions.prompt: A small, well chosen market can be a better start than a giant one.
questions.explain: Facebook started with one college. Winning a small market fully gives you a base to grow.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 checks for a new market.
options: Is it big enough to matter?
Do we have an edge there?
Is the need strong and growing?
Does the CEO like the city?
questions.explain: Size, edge and need. Trends and personal taste aren't strategy.

questions.prompt: Match each company to where it chose to play first.

pairs.right: Active traders who hated high fees
Bike taxis for cheap, quick city trips
Low cost exam prep for students
Beauty shoppers wanting real products online

questions.explain: Each picked a clear group with a clear need that others served badly.

questions.prompt: Which is the weakest reason to enter a market?
lines: Users there have a painful problem
We have special data or partners there
A rival entered it last week
questions.explain: Following a rival isn't a reason by itself.

questions.prompt: Order a classic expansion path.
steps: Prove users love it and money works
Expand to similar cities or groups
questions.explain: Prove it small, then scale. Swiggy grew city by city, then added Instamart.

questions.prompt: What does TAM mean?
options: Total addressable market: everyone who could use it
questions.explain: TAM is the biggest possible market. It's a ceiling, not a forecast.

lessons.title: Reading the competition
teach: Competitors are not just apps like yours. They are anything users use today to solve the same job.
Direct competitors do the same thing (Blinkit vs Zepto). Indirect ones solve the same job differently (the local kirana shop).
Positioning is how you choose to be different: faster, cheaper, more trusted, better for a specific group.

questions.prompt: Match each product to an indirect competitor.

pairs.right: Owning a car or the metro

questions.explain: Indirect rivals solve the same job another way.

questions.prompt: Which is direct competition for Spotify?
questions.explain: Same job, same way: streaming music.

questions.prompt: Netflix's CEO once said their biggest rival is sleep.
questions.explain: Their real fight is for your free time, against anything else you could do with it.

questions.prompt: Which is a weak positioning statement?
lines: The fastest grocery delivery in your area
Zero fee investing for first time investors
Trusted home services with trained professionals
questions.explain: 'Good' doesn't say who it's for or why it's different.

questions.prompt: Blinkit leads. How might Zepto position itself differently?
options: Push its café and young urban users harder
questions.explain: Finding a different strength gives users a reason to choose you.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for a competitor analysis.
steps: Compare on what users care about
Find a gap you can own
questions.explain: Start from the user, not from a list of company names.

questions.prompt: You should only watch companies that look exactly like you.
questions.explain: Disruption often comes from different looking products, like phones replacing cameras.

lessons.title: Big bets and platform moves
teach: Some strategic moves are big bets: entering a new category, building a platform, or going after a new market.
A platform lets others build on you, like Android for app makers or Shopify for shops. It can grow faster than you could alone.
Big bets should connect to your strengths, like users, data, brand or infrastructure you already have.

questions.prompt: Why did Swiggy launch Instamart?
options: It already had riders, users and a delivery habit to reuse
questions.explain: A good bet reuses existing strengths. Riders and app users made grocery delivery a natural step.

questions.prompt: Match each company to its platform move.

pairs.right: Rails any app can build payments on
Tools for players to build games

questions.explain: Each let others build on top, multiplying what users can get.

questions.prompt: A big bet should ideally use strengths the company already has.
questions.explain: Bets far from your strengths fail more often. Many 'super app' attempts struggled for this reason.

questions.prompt: Which bet looks weakest for a food delivery app?
lines: Grocery delivery using the same riders
Ads for restaurants on the app
Dining out deals for existing users
questions.explain: A phone has nothing to do with its strengths and needs totally new skills.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 things to check before a big bet.
options: Can we test it small first?
Will it look good in the news?
questions.explain: Strengths, size and a way to test cheaply before going all in.

questions.prompt: What lesson does BYJU'S teach about big bets?
options: Growing too fast with expensive buys and heavy debt can sink a company
questions.explain: Fast acquisitions and pushy sales grew revenue on paper but hurt trust and cash. Bets need a solid base.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for making a big bet safely.
steps: State the bet and why we can win
questions.explain: Bet small, learn, then decide.

lessons.title: Putting it all together
teach: A full product view connects everything: users and their problem, how money is made, the north star and KPI tree, growth loops, and strategy.
That's exactly what a teardown is. Practise by writing one, then play a product game to check yourself.
In interviews, keep linking back to the user and the goal. That's what makes answers feel like a PM's.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a teardown in a logical order.
questions.explain: From people to money to metrics to strategy to next steps.

questions.prompt: Match each question to the unit that answers it.

pairs.left: Why is the leader hard to beat?

questions.explain: Each unit gives you one lens. Together they explain a whole product.

questions.prompt: In an interview, what makes an answer sound like a PM's?
options: Linking every idea back to a user need and a clear goal
questions.explain: Clear user, clear goal, clear trade-offs. That's product thinking.

questions.prompt: Writing your own teardowns is a great way to build product sense.
questions.explain: Writing forces you to think through each part. Use Prodscope's 'Write your own teardown' to get feedback.

questions.prompt: Which part is missing from this mini teardown of Rapido?
lines: Users: commuters who want cheap, quick trips
Money: subscription fee from drivers instead of commission
North star: completed rides per week
questions.explain: The last line isn't insight. A real teardown would add growth, competition or ideas instead.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 habits that make you a better PM over time.
questions.explain: Curiosity, user contact and data. Frameworks help only when you use them to think.

questions.prompt: You've finished all units. Playing product games is a good next step.
questions.explain: Each game walks a full product from users to crisis. Try to win all 200.
